one_liner: Purely functional data-parallel language compiled to OpenCL/CUDA/HIP/multicore C; PLDI 2017 compared it with hand-written Rodinia, Parboil and FinPar GPU code.
what_it_does: Futhark is an ML-family array language. You write map, reduce, scan, histogram and loop code once, and the Haskell compiler emits C plus OpenCL, CUDA or HIP kernels (or sequential, multicore or ISPC CPU code). With --library it emits a .c/.h pair whose entry points you call from C or C++ (Python and WebAssembly backends also exist). It is not a drop-in for any C++ API: the hot kernel has to be rewritten in Futhark, and arrays move in and out through the generated C API.
how_it_is_fast: The compiler fuses nested SOACs (map-map, map-reduce and streaming combinators), so intermediate arrays are never written to memory. It flattens nested parallelism into GPU kernels and sequentialises the excess inside each thread. It transposes arrays for coalesced access and does simple block tiling in local memory. Uniqueness-typed in-place updates keep sequential inner loops cheap. In the paper's ablation, fusion gave K-means 1.42x, LavaMD 4.55x and LocVolCalib 9.4x; coalescing gave K-means 9.26x and OptionPricing 8.79x; without in-place updates K-means was 8.3x slower.
when_to_use: Regular nested data-parallel kernels (map/reduce/scan nests, segmented reductions, histograms, stencils, Monte Carlo pricing) that you would otherwise write and maintain as hand OpenCL or CUDA
Porting reference GPU code that leaves reductions on the host or lacks coalescing, as Rodinia NN, Backprop and K-means do: Futhark keeps those steps on the device
One source that must target NVIDIA (CUDA/OpenCL), AMD (HIP/OpenCL) and multicore CPUs, called from a C/C++ host through the generated library
Large, batched inputs that keep the GPU busy; the measured runs used megabyte-scale datasets
when_not_to_use: Against well-tuned hand GPU code: the paper's own estimate is 0.79x (geometric mean of CFD, HotSpot, LavaMD and LocVolCalib). Reasons given are unneeded copies, double buffering by copy instead of pointer swap, and no time tiling
Dense linear algebra where cuBLAS or rocBLAS applies: there is no vendor-BLAS path, and open issue #1429 asks for one
Irregular, pointer-based or recursive structures, and mostly sequential code: the language needs regular arrays and bulk operators
Small inputs or many short kernels: the paper blames kernel launch overhead for NN's much smaller win on the AMD GPU
Picking it on these numbers alone: they come from a 2017 compiler on 2013-2014 GPUs, the GTX column has no per-run data in the artifact, and futhark-benchmarks publishes no results

integration.form: compiler (code generator); library mode emits C source plus header to compile into a C/C++ project
integration.dependencies: Futhark compiler (Haskell; binary releases or a GHC build); generated code needs a C compiler plus OpenCL, CUDA or HIP for GPU backends, pthreads for multicore, and ISPC 1.31+ for the ispc backend
integration.min_toolchain: Compiler: futhark.cabal 0.29.0 needs base >= 4.20 (GHC 9.10+). Generated code is plain C
integration.platforms: Generated code: sequential C, multicore C, ISPC, OpenCL, CUDA, HIP, Python/PyOpenCL and WebAssembly backends. The PLDI artifact was tested only on Linux with NVIDIA and AMD GPUs
integration.thread_safety: Partly documented. CHANGELOG #1169 makes futhark_context_clear_caches() and the opaque-free functions thread-safe; general rules for sharing one context across threads were not read this session

gotchas: Harness flaw (K-means): the patched Rodinia timer wraps cluster(), and cluster() calls allocate(). In the yuhc/gpu-rodinia copy of Rodinia 3.1, allocate() creates a new OpenCL context and queue, reads and builds kmeans.cl, allocates buffers and uploads the whole feature matrix on every run. The paper says context creation, kernel build and upload were excluded. The W8100 file shows it: first reference run 1876.9 ms, then 1128.7-1154.6 ms; the mean is 1216.08 ms (1142.66 ms without run 1). The GTX 2.79x (1597.7 vs 572.2 ms) has no per-run data, so its inflation is unknown. futhark kmeans-futhark.runtimes holds 6 runs, not 10.

Workload choice (NN): the artifact patch changes Rodinia's run line from '-r 5' to '-r 100'. That multiplies the reference's sequential CPU findLowest work by 20 (100 linear passes over all records instead of 5), and the timed loop also reads back every distance. Futhark does the 100 argmin reductions on the GPU. The paper attributes the NN gap to exactly those 100 CPU reductions, so the 16x headline rests on this parameter; the dataset table does not say the default was 5.

lavaMD patch adds sleep(3) after each timed reference run (outside the timer). The idle GPU may downclock before each 5-9 ms kernel; the effect was not measured. Myocyte compares Futhark OpenCL with Rodinia's CUDA version, after the patch changed workload 1 to 65536 and mode 0 to 1.

The generated library owns GPU memory through a Futhark context, so data crosses the API as Futhark arrays (copies in and out). Keep data in Futhark values between calls, or the transfer time the paper excluded will dominate.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Futhark over Halide when the kernel is general nested map/reduce/scan code with segmented reductions rather than an image pipeline whose schedule you want to tune by hand. Pick DiffEqGPU.jl for ODE ensembles in Julia, and CBQN for CPU array scripting with no GPU.
verified_claims_summary: PLDI 2017 (Henriksen et al.): 16 benchmarks hand-translated to Futhark (compiler git 78c956b, OpenCL backend, no tuning), 10-run averages on a GTX 780 Ti (CUDA 8.0) and an AMD FirePro W8100. Against hand-written OpenCL (CUDA for Myocyte) from Rodinia 3.1, Parboil 2.5 and FinPar, the geometric mean is 1.81x over 12 benchmarks, from 0.6x (LocVolCalib) to 16x (NN). Futhark is slower on 4 of the 12 (0.79x geometric mean). The four Accelerate rows compare against Accelerate 0.15.1, a Haskell DSL, not C; the artifact keeps only the W8100 per-run data.
status_note: Actively developed (0.28.1 released, 0.29.0 at HEAD, last commit 2026-10-11, ISC, about 2.8k stars) and usable today as a C-emitting GPU code generator. The speed evidence, though, is a 2017 paper whose largest wins come from under-optimised Rodinia references. The artifact (code reading) shows two harness flaws: the K-means reference timer includes per-run OpenCL context creation, kernel build and upload, and NN's top-k count was raised from 5 to 100.
